---
title: How the encryption works
---

Every secret is encrypted in the sender's browser before anything leaves the page, and decrypted in the recipient's browser after the ciphertext arrives. The WordPress server stores an envelope it has no key for. This page walks through exactly what the browser does, what the server receives, and why the server cannot read a secret even if it wanted to.

<!-- wp:docspress/callout {"tone":"success","title":"The server never holds a key","content":"<p>The 256-bit key that protects a secret is generated by the sender's browser and travels only inside the share link's <code>#fragment</code>, which browsers never send in an HTTP request. The key, the pass phrase, and the plaintext are never posted, never logged, and never stored. A create request that carries a field named <code>key</code>, <code>passphrase</code>, <code>secret</code>, <code>plaintext</code>, or <code>message</code> is rejected with <code>400</code> before anything else is looked at.</p>","collapsible":false} /-->

## The trust boundary

Psst is a zero-knowledge design. The browser is the only place plaintext exists, and the link is the only place the key exists.

<!-- wp:docspress/diagram {"title":"Who sees what","type":"sequence","source":"Sender browser -> Sender browser: generate 32-byte key, encrypt with AES-256-GCM\nSender browser -> WordPress: POST /psst/v1/secrets (ciphertext, iv, check)\nWordPress -> Sender browser: 201 id, url, manage_token\nSender browser -> Sender browser: link = url + \"#\" + key\nSender -> Recipient: share link (email, chat, ...)\nRecipient browser -> WordPress: GET /s/{id}/ (fragment is not sent)\nWordPress -> Recipient browser: interstitial page, no ciphertext\nRecipient browser -> WordPress: POST /psst/v1/secrets/{id}/reveal\nWordPress -> WordPress: conditional UPDATE, then hard delete\nWordPress -> Recipient browser: 200 envelope, exactly once\nRecipient browser -> Recipient browser: decrypt with key from #fragment","caption":"The key never crosses the dotted line into WordPress. Everything the server stores is ciphertext plus the parameters needed to decrypt it somewhere else."} /-->

What WordPress can see, and therefore what a database dump, a hosting provider, a compromised admin account, or a subpoena can see:

- The ciphertext, the initialization vector, and the 16-byte check value.
- Whether a pass phrase was used, and if so the PBKDF2 salt and iteration count.
- When the secret was created, when it expires, and whether it has been read.

What WordPress cannot see under any circumstances:

- The 32-byte URL key. It exists in the sender's browser and in the link, nowhere else.
- The pass phrase. It is turned into key material locally and never transmitted.
- The plaintext, before or after encryption.

Administrators see the same thing the database sees. The admin list shows metadata only, and the shred button deletes a row it cannot read.

## The key derivation chain

The browser runs the following chain using the Web Crypto API only. There are no third-party cryptography dependencies. The implementation in `blocks/src/shared/crypto.js` is the single copy of the protocol, and the same file runs unchanged under the Node test runner and the Playwright end-to-end suite.

<!-- wp:docspress/colorful-code {"language":"plaintext","filename":"psst/2 envelope","code":"urlKey  = 32 random bytes                       kept in the link fragment, never sent\nsalt    = 16 random bytes                       only when a pass phrase is set\nppBits  = PBKDF2-SHA-256(NFKC(passphrase), salt, iterations)   or empty\naesKey  = HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = urlKey, salt = ppBits, info = \"psst/2/content\")\nchkKey  = HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = urlKey, salt = ppBits, info = \"psst/2/check\")\ncheck   = HMAC-SHA-256(chkKey, \"psst\")[0..16]\niv      = 12 random bytes\nct      = AES-256-GCM(aesKey, iv, plaintext, aad = \"psst/2;pp=0|1\", tag = 128 bits)","showLineNumbers":true,"caption":"The chain the browser runs for every secret. Lines 2 and 3 are skipped when there is no pass phrase; ppBits is then a zero-length salt."} /-->

### Why the pass phrase is optional

The URL key alone is 256 bits of entropy, which is already beyond brute force. A pass phrase is for a different threat: someone who sees the link in transit. When a pass phrase is set, holding the link is not enough. The recipient must also know something the sender told them through a second channel.

Because the check value is derived from both the URL key and the pass phrase, a holder of the link can test pass-phrase guesses offline against the check. PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations makes each guess expensive. Treat the pass phrase as a second factor for the link, not as the primary protection.

## What is sent when a secret is created

The sender's browser posts one JSON body to `POST /psst/v1/secrets`. The server validates the shape of every field, rejects anything on the forbidden list, and stores the result.

<!-- wp:docspress/api-request {"method":"POST","endpoint":"/wp-json/psst/v1/secrets","headers":"Content-Type: application/json\nAccept: application/json","requestBody":"{\n  \"version\": 2,\n  \"ciphertext\": \"<base64url, plaintext length + 16-byte tag>\",\n  \"iv\": \"<base64url, 12 bytes>\",\n  \"has_passphrase\": true,\n  \"salt\": \"<base64url, 16 bytes>\",\n  \"kdf\": { \"name\": \"PBKDF2\", \"hash\": \"SHA-256\", \"iterations\": 600000 },\n  \"check\": \"<base64url, 16 bytes>\",\n  \"ttl_minutes\": 60,\n  \"hp\": \"\",\n  \"challenge\": null\n}","requestBodyFormat":"json","responseStatus":"201 Created","responseBody":"{\n  \"id\": \"<22 base64url characters>\",\n  \"url\": \"https://example.com/s/<id>/\",\n  \"manage_token\": \"<43 base64url characters, shown once>\",\n  \"expires_at\": \"2026-06-01T19:00:00+00:00\",\n  \"expires_in\": 3600,\n  \"expires_label\": \"June 1, 2026 @ 3:00 pm\",\n  \"has_passphrase\": true,\n  \"ttl_minutes\": 60\n}","responseBodyFormat":"json","runnable":false,"editable":false,"allowUnsafe":false,"timeout":10000} /-->

Notice what is absent. There is no key, no pass phrase, and no plaintext. The browser then builds the share link by joining the returned URL and the key it kept:

```text
https://example.com/s/<id>/#<43-character key>
```

Everything before the `#` is the address of the envelope. Everything after it is the only thing that can open the envelope, and browsers strip it before sending any request. The viewer also accepts the form `#k=<key>` for forward compatibility.

Requests are sent with `credentials: 'omit'`, so no WordPress cookies travel with them. A logged-in administrator who creates a secret is indistinguishable from an anonymous sender.

## What is stored

The server rewrites the create body into a stored envelope and keeps it as the post content of a private `psst_secret` post. The field names differ from the request, which matters if you are reading the database or the reveal response.

<!-- wp:docspress/fields {"title":"Stored envelope","description":"The JSON returned by the reveal call and the only thing the database holds about a secret's content.","fields":[{"name":"v","type":"number","required":true,"defaultValue":"2","description":"Protocol version. The viewer refuses anything else.","values":"2","deprecated":false},{"name":"alg","type":"string","required":true,"defaultValue":"A256GCM","description":"The cipher. The viewer refuses anything else.","values":"A256GCM","deprecated":false},{"name":"aad","type":"string","required":true,"defaultValue":"","description":"The additional authenticated data the sender used. The viewer recomputes it from <code>kdf</code> and rejects a mismatch before attempting decryption.","values":"psst/2;pp=0, psst/2;pp=1","deprecated":false},{"name":"iv","type":"string","required":true,"defaultValue":"","description":"12 bytes, base64url.","values":"","deprecated":false},{"name":"ct","type":"string","required":true,"defaultValue":"","description":"Ciphertext with the 16-byte GCM tag appended, base64url.","values":"","deprecated":false},{"name":"kdf","type":"object","required":false,"defaultValue":"null","description":"<code>{ name, hash, iterations, salt }</code> when a pass phrase was set. The salt moves inside this object in the stored form.","values":"","deprecated":false},{"name":"check","type":"string","required":true,"defaultValue":"","description":"16 bytes, base64url. Used locally by the recipient to distinguish a wrong pass phrase from corruption.","values":"","deprecated":false}]} /-->

The post type is not public, is excluded from search, sitemaps, archives, and the core REST API, and its content is never rendered by a template. The end-to-end suite asserts that the rendered viewer page does not contain the ciphertext.

## How a reveal works

The reveal is the only operation that consumes a secret, and it is designed so that only a deliberate click in the viewer can trigger it.

<!-- wp:docspress/flow {"start":1,"steps":[{"title":"The recipient opens the link","content":"<p>The browser requests <code>/s/{id}/</code>. The fragment stays in the address bar. The server does a read-only lookup and renders an interstitial with a heading, an intro, a pass-phrase field if one is needed, and a <strong>View Secret</strong> button. No ciphertext is in the page.</p>"},{"title":"Nothing is consumed yet","content":"<p>Link previewers, mail scanners, and security proxies fetch the page with <code>GET</code>. Reloading the page, or opening it in three tabs, changes nothing. The end-to-end tests assert zero reveal requests until the button is clicked.</p>"},{"title":"The recipient clicks View","content":"<p>The viewer reads the key from <code>location.hash</code>, then sends <code>POST /psst/v1/secrets/{id}/reveal</code> with <code>Content-Type: application/json</code> and no cookies. The server answers <code>415</code> to any other content type, which rules out HTML form posts.</p>"},{"title":"The server hands over the envelope exactly once","content":"<p>The claim is a single conditional <code>UPDATE</code> that flips the row out of <code>publish</code>. Only the caller whose update changed exactly one row receives the envelope; every other caller, including a concurrent one, receives <code>404</code>. The row is then hard-deleted in the same request.</p>"},{"title":"The browser decrypts","content":"<p>The viewer validates <code>v</code>, <code>alg</code>, and <code>aad</code>, derives the keys, compares the check value, and only then runs AES-GCM. On success it shows the plaintext and calls <code>history.replaceState</code> to drop the fragment from the URL and the browser history.</p>"}]} /-->

### Wrong pass phrase versus corrupted envelope

Because the reveal is one-shot, a typo in the pass phrase cannot be allowed to destroy the secret. The viewer keeps the envelope in memory after the first reveal and checks pass-phrase attempts against the check value locally. A wrong pass phrase produces a retry prompt with no further network request. The end-to-end suite asserts that a wrong attempt followed by a correct one totals exactly one reveal call.

| Condition | Result in the viewer | Network calls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correct key, no pass phrase needed | Plaintext shown | 1 |
| Correct key, wrong pass phrase | "That pass phrase did not unlock the secret. Try again.", field refocused | 1 total |
| Correct key, correct pass phrase on retry | Plaintext shown | still 1 |
| Key missing from the URL | "This link is missing its key. Ask the sender to send the full link again." before any request | 0 |
| Altered ciphertext, IV, or additional data | "This secret could not be decrypted. The link may have been altered." | 1 |
| Key for a different secret | "This secret could not be decrypted. The link may have been altered." | 1 |
| Secret already read, expired, or shredded | "This secret is no longer available." | 1, answered 404 |

## What the tests prove

The claims on this page are asserted by the checked-in test suites rather than by documentation alone.

- **Unit tests** in `blocks/src/shared/__tests__/crypto.test.js` cover the RFC 4648 base64url vectors, both fragment forms, round trips with and without a pass phrase, wrong and missing pass phrases raising before any AES-GCM attempt, a single flipped ciphertext byte and a flipped additional-data flag both failing as corruption, and two encryptions of the same text producing different ciphertext and check values.
- **REST tests** in `tests/e2e/rest.spec.mjs` create a secret with the real browser crypto module, confirm the rendered page carries `noindex` and `no-store` and does not contain the ciphertext, confirm the reveal returns byte-identical values, confirm a second reveal is `404`, confirm a form-encoded reveal is `415` and consumes nothing, and confirm a request carrying a `passphrase` field is refused.
- **Flow tests** in `tests/e2e/secret-flow.spec.mjs` open links in a cookie-less browser context, count every reveal request, and confirm that the interstitial and a reload consume nothing, that the fragment is gone after reveal, and that a shredded or already-read link renders only the gone state.

Run them with the commands in [Development](../reference/development.md).

## Limits of the model

Zero knowledge on the server does not mean zero risk everywhere. Be clear with senders about what the design does not cover.

- **The link is the secret.** Anyone who obtains the full link before the recipient opens it can read the secret. Pass phrases mitigate this; sending the link and the pass phrase through different channels mitigates it further.
- **The browser is trusted.** A compromised browser, a malicious extension, or a modified copy of the viewer script can read the plaintext. Serving the site over HTTPS and enabling the optional Content-Security-Policy header in [Hardening](hardening.md) reduce the ways the script can be altered in transit.
- **Secure context required.** Browsers expose the Web Crypto API only on HTTPS origins and `localhost`. On a plain HTTP site both blocks render an "unsupported" message and refuse to run.
- **Metadata is visible.** The server knows a secret exists, how large the ciphertext is, when it was created, and when it was read or expired. It does not know what it said.
